---
order: 1
unit: layers
title: Reading the layers
node: AC9HH7K08 n1
assumes:
  - AC9HH7K01
  - AC9HH7K07
summary: Read an excavation as a sequence of layers. Use the position of a find and the evidence beside it to explain what may have changed, while keeping relative age separate from an exact date.
language: maths
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8720
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8720/index.html
  readySelector: "#gpanel"
  layout: full
explainClip:
  query: { code: "@dig.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain }
  caption: "How layers build up"
  say: "How layers build up at a site."
  clip:
    - caption: { text: "At a site, layers build up over time.", say: "At a site, layers of soil and rubbish build up over time." }
    - wait: 600
    - click: Lay down the next layer
    - caption: { text: "Layer A goes down first.", say: "Layer A goes down first." }
    - wait: 700
    - click: Lay down the next layer
    - caption: { text: "Then B on top of it.", say: "Then layer B goes on top of it." }
    - wait: 700
    - click: Lay down the next layer
    - caption: { text: "Then C. The top layer is the youngest.", say: "Then layer C. The top layer is the youngest." }
    - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "bottom one formed first" }
    - wait: 900
    - click: Dig the pit
    - caption: { text: "Later, someone digs a pit down into A.", say: "Later, someone digs a pit down through the layers into A." }
    - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "younger than the layers it cuts" }
    - wait: 700
    - caption: { text: "The coin in the pit is deep, but it is young.", say: "The coin in the pit is deep, but it is younger than those layers." }
    - wait: 1500
hook: Two pieces of pottery look alike. One is in the bottom layer and one is near the surface. What would you need to know before calling one older?
---
When soil, rubbish and building rubble pile up at a place over time, they form layers. Studying those layers is called **stratigraphy**. If nothing has dug into the layers or mixed them up, the lower ones were laid down first. So the layers tell you an order (this one is older than that one), but not a date in years. That is why archaeologists write down exactly where each thing was found, not just what it is.

**A real site:** UNESCO's [page on the First Qin Emperor's mausoleum](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/441) describes the clay figures, horses, chariots and weapons found there. The dig below is **made up**. It is not the record of that site or any real site in China. Read it from the surface down.

![A made-up excavation with three undisturbed layers: C at the top, B in the middle and A at the bottom.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Layer | Finds |
|---|---|
| C, top | A new floor and cooking pots |
| B, middle | Charcoal and burnt roof wood |
| A, bottom | An earlier floor and pottery |

Nothing has dug into these layers or mixed them up.

## Predict: which came first?

```step
stage: predict
insight: Students commit to a rule for reading layers before they test it.
check:
  type: predict
  q: Which layer formed first?
  options:
    - C, the top layer
    - B, the middle layer
    - A, the bottom layer
  actual: A formed first. Nothing has disturbed these layers, so B was laid on top of A, then C on top of B.
```

## Try: order or date?

```step
stage: run
insight: Students separate claims about order from claims about dates before using layers as evidence.
check:
  type: sort
  q: Is each sentence about the order of the layers, or about an exact date?
  options:
    - Relative order
    - Exact date
  items:
    - - A formed before B
      - Relative order
      - It compares two layers.
    - - The fire happened in 220 BCE
      - Exact date
      - That needs a year, and the layers on their own cannot give you one.
    - - C formed after B
      - Relative order
      - The new floor is above the burnt material.
```

Was your guess right? Layers can tell you "before" and "after". They cannot tell you "how many years".

## Practise: dig it yourself

Now dig the same made-up site from the top down. You reach the newest layer first.

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Digging from the top down, then numbering the layers from the oldest, turns 'lower is older' into something students do, not only read."
try: { playground: board, starter: "dig.yml#dig", height: 520 }
hint: ["Which layer did you reach last?", "Nothing has disturbed these layers, so the one at the bottom was laid down before the others."]
check: { type: board, text: "Dig down to the bottom, then number the layers from the one that formed first.", when: "in_order = 1", explain: "A, at the bottom, formed first, then B, then C on top. You dug them in the opposite order: the newest comes off first." }
```

## Worked example: what happened here?

```step
stage: investigate
insight: Students make the main inference from the layers, then repair the planted misconception that depth gives an exact age.
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: Which story fits the layers best?
      options:
        - The new floor was laid before the earlier floor
        - A fire may have happened between two periods of use
        - An invading army probably burned the place down
      answer: 1
      explain: An earlier floor, then burnt material, then a new floor. That fits people using the place, a fire, then people using it again. What caused the fire is still an open question.
      feedback:
        - That reads the layers upside down. The earlier floor is in layer A, at the bottom, so it came first.
        - null
        - That guesses a cause. Charcoal shows something burned. It does not show who or what started the fire.
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Nib writes: “B is deeper than C, so B is exactly 500 years older.” What needs changing?"
      options:
        - Keep the order but take out the 500 years
        - Swap the order, because deeper layers are newer
        - Keep the 500 years, because three layers prove it
      answer: 0
      explain: Being deeper tells you B is older here. It does not tell you by how many years.
      feedback:
        - null
        - Nothing has disturbed these layers, so the lower one formed first.
        - A layer can build up in a week or over centuries. Counting layers does not give years.
      fault: logic
      misconception: layers-give-exact-date
    smaller:
      check:
        type: question
        q: Can a stack of layers on its own tell you how many years passed?
        options:
          - Yes, count the layers
          - No, it only tells you the order
        answer: 1
        explain: The order is still useful, even when we do not know how long it took.
        feedback:
          - Some layers form fast (a flood) and some slowly. Counting them does not give years.
          - null
    hint:
      - Is Nib putting the layers in order, or measuring time?
      - What extra evidence would you need to put years on this sequence?
```

The earlier floor is below the burnt material, and a later floor is above it. A fire between two periods of use is one way to read that. The burnt material on its own does not show who started the fire or whether there was an attack.

## Vary: a pit cuts through

Now change one thing. Later on, someone digs a pit down through layers C and B into A. A recent coin falls into the soil that fills the pit. The coin ends up deep, but the pit is younger than every layer it cuts through.

```step
stage: modify
insight: Students see that the deeper-is-older rule only works when the layers have not been disturbed.
try: { playground: board, starter: "dig.yml#pit", height: 520 }
tasks:
  - check:
      type: board
      text: "Find the thing that is out of place. Click it and say how its age compares with the layer around it."
      when: "n_found = 1 and n_stray = 0"
      explain: "The coin fell into the pit, and the pit was dug after every layer it cuts through. So the coin is younger than layer A, even though it is just as deep."
    hint: ["Which find is not in a layer, but in the pit?", "The pit was dug after the layers. What does that make anything that fell into it?"]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: Before you use the coin's depth to say how old it is, what should you record?
      options:
        - That it lay as deep as layer A, so it is as old as A
        - That it was found inside the later pit
        - The year on the coin, which gives the age of layer A
      answer: 1
      explain: The pit has disturbed the layers. If you only looked at depth, you would think the coin was old.
      feedback:
        - That treats the coin as the same age as the layer around it. It fell into a pit dug later, so depth tells you nothing about its age here.
        - null
        - That treats the coin's year as the layer's year. The coin is in the pit, not in layer A, and the pit was dug long after A formed.
```

## Practise: a new site

```step
stage: practise
insight: Students apply the same reasoning to a new case on their own.
check:
  type: question
  q: At a second made-up site, nothing has been disturbed. A floor lies under a layer of flood mud, and a rebuilt wall sits on top of the mud. Which story do the layers support?
  options:
    - A flood came first, and then people laid the floor on the mud
    - The rebuilt wall shows what caused the flood in the first place
    - People used the floor, then a flood came, then they rebuilt
  answer: 2
  explain: The positions give you an order. They do not tell you the cause or the year.
  feedback:
    - That reads the layers upside down. The floor is under the flood mud, so it came first.
    - That asks the layers for a cause. A wall built afterwards cannot tell you what caused the flood.
    - null
```

## Make: explain it in your own book

```step
stage: make
insight: Students write an explanation that names evidence and a limit, read by a person.
check:
  type: reflect
  text: In my own book I drew three layers for a made-up site, put one find in each, and wrote two sentences about their order and one thing the layers cannot tell me. A partner read it and gave feedback.
```

Write in your own book or document. Say what you think happened, which layer shows it, and one thing the layers cannot tell you. Your partner or teacher reads it; this page only keeps your tick.

## Typical: weapons in the charcoal

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: Students meet another find in the same sequence and keep the claim within the evidence.
check:
  type: question
  q: The charcoal layer also has broken weapons in it. Which sentence stays within the evidence?
  options:
    - Weapons and burning raise an attack as a question, not an answer
    - An attack probably happened, since weapons and fire go together
    - The weapons tell you the exact year the fire happened
  answer: 0
  explain: Weapons and burning together make an attack worth looking into. They do not settle the cause.
  feedback:
    - null
    - "That still treats the weapons as proof, just more softly. Weapons could have been stored there, or dropped long before the fire."
    - Weapons need their own dating evidence. Finding them does not give a year.
```

## Typical: a coin in the layers

A coin can tell you something about when a layer formed, but only so much. Coins were used for years, so a coin can already be old when someone drops it.

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "A dated find gives the earliest its own layer could have formed, and the layers above it too, but says nothing certain about the layers below."
try: { playground: board, starter: "dig.yml#date", height: 560 }
hint: ["Could the coin have been dropped before it was made?", "Could the layers under the coin's layer have formed before 220 BCE, after it, or either?"]
check: { type: board, text: "For each layer, choose: formed in 220 BCE or later, or can't tell from the coin.", when: "n_right = 3 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "Layer B can't be older than the coin in it, so it formed in 220 BCE or later, and so did C on top of it. Layer A formed before B, but the coin doesn't say when: it could be from long before 220 BCE." }
```

## Wider: draw the pit

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: Students test the limit of the deeper-is-older rule by drawing and explaining a disturbance.
check:
  type: reflect
  text: I added a later pit to my drawing, marked where it cuts older layers, and explained to a partner why a deep object in its filling could be recent.
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
learning: use undisturbed layers to put finds in order, without reading depth as
  an exact date
summary: Read an excavation as a sequence of layers. Use the position of a find
  and the evidence beside it to explain what may have changed, while keeping
  relative age separate from an exact date.
goals:
  - I can use undisturbed layers to put finds in relative order.
  - I can use finds to suggest a change and name a limit.
struggle: Depth feels like a clock. Ask students to separate “before” from “how
  many years before” before giving them a date.
before: >-
  This is the first K08 hinge: without the logic of layers, the scientific and
  written evidence in lessons 2 and 3 becomes a collection of facts rather than
  evidence in a sequence. All excavation cards are invented. The diagram is
  schematic, not to scale. Keep “undisturbed” attached to the deeper-is-older
  rule. The wider pit case shows why.


  Usually Year 7; not yet tried with a class. The untiered path is the minimum.
  Time and optional width are the teacher’s choices.


  Across subjects: Year 7 Geography's "How moving water changes the land"
  (`geography/water-7/water-changes-land`) shows where layers come from: water
  carries sediment and drops it where the flow slows (deposition). Same year, so
  it's a mention, not a link. Year 8 science's rock cycle uses the same
  layers-in-order idea later and can look back here.


  The dig board (1 Nov 2026) is a made-up site seen from the side: students dig
  from the top down and number the layers from the oldest, find the coin that
  fell into a later pit, and (Typical) decide what a coin made in 220 BCE can
  and cannot date. The board only checks these planted answers. Its model is
  undisturbed layers unless a pit is shown; say so if students ask about real
  sites, where animals, roots, floods and later digging can mix layers. The
  Explain it to me clip shows layers building up and a pit cut through them
  (about 20 seconds, captions first).


  K08 lists AC9HH7K01 and AC9HH7K07 as prior knowledge. Use their curriculum
  pointer pages (teacher view: /teach/curriculum/history/AC9HH7K01/ and
  /teach/curriculum/history/AC9HH7K07/; the student lesson no longer links to
  them), rather than adding our own First Nations explanations. Start with
  ACARA’s elaborations on that pointer page and ask the school’s First Nations
  contact for local, community-approved material. Do not treat this methods
  course as covering K07.


  Relevant ACARA K08 elaboration (an example, not a checklist): “creating a
  cross-sectional drawing of the earth's surface from an archaeological
  excavation to identify the evidence located at various layers (stratigraphy)
  and what it reveals about change over time; for example, a charcoal layer
  containing human remains and weapons may indicate the capture and destruction
  of an ancient settlement such as Troy”
running:
  - "Predict and Try: ask students to give a reason before revealing the
    explanation."
  - "Dig it yourself (board): put it up and dig together first. Ask: which layer
    did we reach last, and why is it the oldest?"
  - "Worked example: use the smaller lead-in if the main distinction is still
    insecure."
  - "Vary and Practise: change one condition and ask what remains supported. On
    the pit board, ask what was dug first, the layers or the pit."
  - "Typical coin step: the hard part is the layer below. A coin gives the
    earliest date its own layer and those above could have formed; it says
    nothing certain about older layers underneath."
  - "Make: a partner or teacher judges the explanation in the student’s own
    book."
stuck:
  - see: "Nib writes: “B is deeper than C, so B is exactly 500 years older.” What
      needs changing?"
    ask: Can a stack of layers alone tell you how many years passed?
    fix: Depth can establish relative order here. It does not measure a number of
      years.
  - see: A student gives a conclusion without saying what supports it.
    ask: Which part of the record supports that?
    fix: Name the source or method, then one thing it cannot settle.
  - see: A student says the layer under the coin is from 220 BCE too.
    ask: Could the coin have been old when it was dropped? Could the layer under it
      be older than the coin?
    fix: The coin dates its own layer and those above (that year or later). Layers
      below formed earlier, by an amount the coin cannot tell you.
support: Use three stacked cards labelled earlier floor, burnt wood, later
  floor. Read one pair at a time before the complete sequence.
stretch: The extra cases add weapons and a later pit. They test the same
  inference with more evidence or a disturbance, without moving to later
  standards.
leads: Continue to DNA and dating answer different questions.
exit:
  q: What can you infer from burnt wood between two floors, and what can you not
    yet say?
  a: A burning event may lie between two periods of use. The cause, exact date and
    time gap need more evidence.
explain: In an undisturbed sequence, lower layers formed first. Finds and their
  positions help reconstruct change; depth alone supplies neither an exact year
  nor a cause.
sources:
  - title: "UNESCO: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor"
    url: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/441
    checked: 2026-10-30
  - title: "Stratigraphy: reading the layers"
    url: https://archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/archeo-sous-marine/en/glossaire/stratigraphy
    checked: 2026-10-30
  - title: "Smithsonian Human Origins: dating"
    url: https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/dating
    checked: 2026-10-30
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Does finding burnt wood prove there was an attack?
    prompts:
      - Which evidence would you need?
      - What would make you change your conclusion?
    notes: Accept competing views where their evidence and limits are stated. Return
      to this question after Make.
  activities:
    - at: investigate
      kind: activity
      title: Try the reasoning together
      do: Lay three paper strips on a desk as layers. Place a small find on each. Ask
        a partner to describe the sequence, then cut a paper pit through them
        and explain what changed.
      notes: Use made-up cases. Check reasons, not speed.
  questions:
    - at: make
      title: Check before moving on
      type: question
      q: At a second made-up, undisturbed site, a floor lies below flood mud and a
        rebuilt wall lies above it. Which account is supported?
      options:
        - A flood came first, then people laid a floor on the mud
        - The rebuilt wall shows what caused the flood
        - People used the floor, then a flood, then they rebuilt
      answer: 2
      explain: The positions give a sequence. They do not give the cause or an exact
        year.
      feedback:
        - The floor is below the flood deposit.
        - A wall does not explain the cause of a flood.
        - null
```

# region: dig
widget: dig
mode: order
site: A made-up dig
note: Nothing has dug into these layers or mixed them up.
layer C: new floor, cooking pots
layer B: charcoal, burnt roof wood
layer A: earlier floor, pottery
dig: on
# endregion

# region: pit
widget: dig
mode: pit
site: The same made-up dig, later
note: Someone has dug a pit down through C and B into A.
layer C: new floor, cooking pots
layer B: charcoal, burnt roof wood
layer A: earlier floor, pottery
pit: C-A, coin
# endregion

mode: date

note: Nothing has disturbed these layers. A coin made in 220 BCE lies in layer B.
layer C: later floor, cups

layer A: early floor, grinding stone

# endregion
